item.title: Extraterrestrial detection inspired by firefly communications could distinguish alien signals from pulsars
item.description: When we think of extraterrestrial intelligence that might be out there among the stars, we tend to think of creatures not too unlike us, though maybe with gray skin, probably bald and with big black eyes. We focus on the familiar, humanoids. But there are many intelligent species on Earth that are nonhumanoid: dolphins, crows, pigs and—with swarm if not individual intelligence—ants and bees. The film "Arrival" conceived of hexapod beings more capable than humans and with a more sophisticated communication system. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Resident experience matters in estimating neighborhood walkability, study shows
item.description: Walking has been shown to improve the overall health of a community and can predict the prevalence of chronic diseases, such as obesity, diabetes and cardiovascular disease, according to the World Health Organization. Because of this, city planners assess neighborhoods' walkability, which measures how built environments support walking, when planning improvements. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Flying‑foxes are starving. Why are we still responding one crisis at a time?
item.description: Once again, Australia's flying-foxes are in trouble. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Confirming altermagnetism: A geometric twist offers experimental proof
item.description: For decades, physicists recognized only two types of magnetism that occur in materials without external influence: ferromagnetism and antiferromagnetism. In findings published in Science, a team led by the U.S. Department of Energy's SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory has delivered conclusive experimental proof of a third magnetic phase called altermagnetism. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Type 2 diabetes breakthrough as 54% achieve remission in just 6 months
item.description: A promising new study suggests that more than half of younger adults with type 2 diabetes could achieve remission in just six months through a combination of a low-calorie diet and structured exercise. Researchers found that 54% of participants under age 45 who followed an intensive diet and exercise program achieved remission, compared with just 4% receiving usual care. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Long-standing Indigenous practice of adding shells to sand helps young clams withstand ocean acidification
item.description: New research from the University of California, Davis, reveals why adding crushed shells to beach sand helps protect shell-making animals—such as clams, oysters and mussels—from the detrimental effects of ocean acidification. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Burrowing shrimp are on the move in a mudflat near you
item.description: Burrowing shrimp are a pest well known to shellfish growers. These pale-bodied creatures excavate mud as they dig into the ground, creating piles of sediment that suffocate oysters and clams growing on the surface. In estuaries on the West Coast, shrimp beds reach densities of hundreds of shrimp per square meter, but the boundaries of the beds change. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Physicists created a tiny universe and watched time emerge without a clock
item.description: Scientists have created a miniature universe in the laboratory that could help answer one of the biggest mysteries in physics: What is time, and where does it come from? Using 24,000 ultracold atoms, a University of Birmingham researcher built an isolated quantum system that repeatedly expands and contracts, mimicking the Big Bang and a possible Big Crunch. Remarkably, the experiment showed that time could emerge from changes happening inside the system, without relying on an external clock. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Unusual quantum states in six-layer graphene offer clues to superconductivity
item.description: Graphene, a material consisting of a sheet of carbon atoms arranged in a honeycomb pattern, has proved promising for various technological applications. Materials in which several layers of graphene are stacked together can exhibit different advantageous properties. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Reexamining sexual and species recognition in butterflies: The Partner-Hazard Space framework
item.description: Generally, intra- and intersexual interactions have been considered qualitatively different processes. However, same-sex sexual behavior is widespread in the animal kingdom, challenging this assumption. Recently, a hypothesis was proposed that regards territorial contests in butterflies, in which two males chase each other without apparent physical attack, as an initial phase of mating behavior. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The asteroid killed the dinosaurs. Why did crocodiles survive?
item.description: Scientists may have solved a 66-million-year-old mystery: how crocodiles survived the asteroid that wiped out the dinosaurs. A sweeping analysis of fossils and ancient climates suggests that their preference for warm environments placed them in tropical refuges that remained habitable even after the catastrophic impact. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Asking teachers to set high expectations leads to more detailed feedback and reveals subtle bias, study finds
item.description: Prompting teachers to communicate high expectations and confidence in students' potential leads them to give more detailed feedback, according to a new study led by Yasemin Copur-Gencturk, Ph.D., a professor of education at USC Rossier and co-director of the USC STEM Center; Ian Thacker, Ph.D., an associate professor of educational psychology at The University of Texas at San Antonio; and Joseph Cimpian, Ph.D., a professor of economics and education policy at New York University. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A computer scientist breaks through a limit that stood since 1996
item.description: A computer scientist has achieved a breakthrough in a nearly 25-year-old problem involving how computers calculate distances across enormous networks. The new algorithm delivers more reliable estimates for closely connected points without sacrificing speed, overcoming a longstanding limitation of earlier methods. Its secret lies in a smarter way of sampling network connections at multiple scales. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Rocket Report: Winter is coming for Themis; Cowboy Space adds iron to the fire
item.description: It's been a good week for ULA with a big NASA contract and Vulcan nearing return-to-flight. Fuente: Ars Technica.

item.title: Most influencers should swear off profanity
item.description: If you spend time watching online videos, you might feel like covering your ears. For some influencers, dropping f-bombs and other swear words is part of their brand, and their followers embrace it. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Cuando pienses que la cera de tus oídos es molesta y asquerosa, piensa que sería peor tener insectos ahí dentro
item.description: El cerumen que se acumula en nuestros oídos para muchas personas es asqueroso e innecesario, puesto que puede generar tapones que nos generan una disminución en la capacidad de escucha. Pero aunque para un buen grupo de la población la cera de los oídos es sinónimo de una falta de higiene, para la biología es un sofisticado sistema de seguridad biomecánico que evita que los insectos colonicen nuestro oído. Dos propiedades. Tras estudiar el cerumen de nuestros oídos, los investigadores han entendido la compleja mecánica que hay detrás, puesto que se ha visto que tiene dos propiedades que… Fuente: Xataka.
item.dc:creator: José A. Lizana

item.title: Hubble reveals a stunning twist in how the universe emerged from darkness
item.description: A surprising discovery by astronomers using the Hubble Space Telescope is challenging a leading explanation for how the early universe emerged from a dense fog of hydrogen roughly 13 billion years ago. Scientists once believed powerful winds from exploding stars helped radiation escape galaxies and clear that cosmic fog, but new observations reveal that these winds actually block radiation instead. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Scientists reveal a hidden snakebite crisis killing up to 513,000 people a year
item.description: A startling new study suggests that venomous snakebites are killing far more people worldwide than official statistics indicate, with an estimated 274,000 to 513,000 deaths every year. Researchers found that as many as 7 million people could suffer snake envenoming annually, while more than 800,000 survivors are left with long-term disabilities. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Why some “lower-risk” childhood cancers turn deadly
item.description: Scientists have uncovered hidden aggressive cancer cells in children whose tumors were previously considered lower risk, revealing why some cases of rhabdomyosarcoma become unexpectedly deadly. The discovery could help doctors identify dangerous tumors earlier and develop personalized treatments that improve survival while reducing unnecessary chemotherapy. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: High-speed microscopy captures 3D images of living cells nearly 400 times faster
item.description: Researchers at the University of Tokyo have developed a high-speed microscopy technique that captures images so quickly they can be used to make "videos" of the dynamic processes that occur inside living cells. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Asian scientists are looking to South Korea as it becomes harder to stay in the US
item.description: As tightening US visa restrictions and geopolitics lock out Asian researchers from Western institutions, South Korea is emerging as a new academic sanctuary for top talent. According to Yoo Ji-beom, president of Sungkyunkwan University (SKKU) in Seoul, that reflects a broader trend that has seen the West giving way to Asia after decades of dominance – particularly in the field of applied technology in China, Japan and South Korea. “Technological competition and global talent mobility are... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Holly Chik

item.title: Crowding can speed up enzyme reactions—until protein droplets become too packed
item.description: Our cells are a hotbed of activity, with reactions churning away to keep us alive. But the cytoplasm, where many metabolic reactions take place, is not uniform. Instead, proteins and other molecules cluster together into membraneless compartments, creating distinct, crowded microenvironments for reactions. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: November’s Night Sky Notes: Light-Day Away
item.description: Twin Travelers In 1977, NASA launched twin spacecraft Voyager 1 and 2, taking advantage of a once-every-175-year planetary alignment of the four largest planets in our solar system: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune. Using six gravity assists between them, this Grand Tour gave us up-close views of the gas and ice giants, including several moons. […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Earth from Space: Champi’s eerie eye
item.description: Image: This image of Super Typhoon Champi from Copernicus Sentinel-3 was captured on 21 October 2026 off the coasts of Taiwan and the Philippines. Fuente: European Space Agency.

item.title: Astronauts just gave the International Space Station a powerful upgrade
item.description: Two astronauts completed a 7-hour, 11-minute spacewalk to install a new solar array on the International Space Station, bringing NASA one step closer to a major power upgrade. Once the final array is installed on November 5, the station will have up to 30% more available power, supporting critical operations and its eventual controlled deorbit. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Small molecular twists may strengthen nature's magnetic compass
item.description: A collaborative research team led by Yasuhiro Kobori at Kobe University, together with researchers from Toho University, Saitama University, Nagoya Institute of Technology and the University of Freiburg, has identified a potential molecular mechanism that could enhance magnetic compass responses in cryptochrome, a blue-light-sensitive protein implicated in magnetoreception. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Vega Island Frozen in Fright
item.description: The sight of an icy skull-like visage on the Antarctic island could make one’s blood run cold. Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Scientists confirm global warming is accelerating faster than ever recorded
item.description: Earth is warming faster than ever recorded, with scientists detecting a major acceleration in global temperatures since around 2015. A new study reveals that the warming rate has surged to approximately 0.35°C per decade, nearly double the average pace observed from 1970 to 2015. After removing natural climate fluctuations, researchers confirmed the acceleration with more than 98% statistical confidence. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: A mysterious star system just 16 light-years away may be hiding habitable planets
item.description: Astronomers have solved a 170-year-old planetary mystery in a nearby two-star system, discovering that a mysterious wobble was caused by stellar activity rather than a giant planet. Although Jupiter-sized worlds have been ruled out in key regions, smaller, potentially habitable planets could still be waiting to be discovered just 16 light-years from Earth. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Space station experiment to probe plant disease risks for future moon and Mars missions
item.description: As NASA and its partners prepare for longer human missions beyond Earth, University of Florida researchers are investigating a challenge that could affect astronauts' ability to grow fresh food in space: plant disease. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Restoration efforts are working, but we need to move faster to meet targets, says U.N. report
item.description: A U.N. report finds that 252 million hectares (ha) (623 million acres) across 149 countries are being restored, creating more than 1 million green jobs—the largest documented global restoration effort to date. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Lab-aged microplastics enable tests of interactions with contaminants
item.description: A newly published study advances our knowledge of how microplastics may age in the environment and whether they stick to other contaminants as they do so. Microplastics (MPs) are tiny plastic pieces that measure less than 5 millimeters (about 0.2 inches) in length. The study looked at the aging of MPs made of three common polymer chemicals—polyethylene, polyethylene terephthalate and polypropylene—to see if they changed as they aged and how that affected nearby contaminants. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists discover mysterious seahorse lookalikes that no one has ever seen alive
item.description: Scientists have discovered that three bizarre deep-sea fish that look exactly like seahorses actually belong to a separate evolutionary group, proving that nature created the same unusual body shape more than once. Nicknamed "sea muppets," these elusive creatures are known from just seven specimens, and no one has ever seen one alive. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: New AI tool helps scientists identify bacteria hidden in soil
item.description: A handful of soil holds a crowded world of bacteria, fungi and other organisms. Scientists can collect their DNA, but much of it remains difficult to identify. Now, researchers at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem and partner institutions have developed an artificial intelligence tool that helps make sense of this genetic puzzle. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New X-ray method isolates faint signals from water at material surfaces
item.description: A research team from Toyohashi University of Technology, the Institute for Molecular Science and the Institute of Science Tokyo, led by Yu Kinjo and professor Ryugo Tero of Toyohashi University of Technology, has developed a new method to investigate the state of water near material surfaces using X-rays. By combining X-ray absorption spectroscopy with data analysis, the researchers separated the weak signals of interfacial water from those of the much larger amount of surrounding water. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New travel tool combines three algorithms to tailor destination recommendations
item.description: Researchers have developed a tourist recommendation system combining three algorithms to help travelers find destinations suited to their preferences, budgets and travel routes. Details appear in the International Journal of Work Innovation and address a limitation of digital platforms that often prioritize popularity over practical considerations. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA's new UV space telescope will launch in 2031
item.description: Most of us could spend our entire lives looking at the night sky and see very few changes. The moon becomes more or less illuminated, the planets drift placidly through the sky, satellites and the ISS intrude for a few moments at a time, and the bright, momentary streak of a meteor punctuates the occasional evening of stargazing. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists discover why chronic back pain feels so personal
item.description: A surprising discovery at UC San Diego suggests that chronic lower back pain may become deeply embedded in the brain's sense of personal identity. Researchers found that movement-triggered pain activates a brain network associated with self-awareness and memories, even though ordinary acute pain typically shuts this network down. This unexpected difference could explain why conventional pain medications often provide limited relief and why fear, anticipation, and past experiences can intensify chronic pain. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Study: Partisan ties shape how voters view campaign AI
item.description: As political campaigns increasingly use artificial intelligence to communicate with voters, questions arise about how the technology influences perceptions of election fairness and trust. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Map Showing Potential Origins of Martian Meteorite Teghaza 001
item.description: Description This global map of Mars shows 13 locations that match the mineralogy and chemistry of Teghaza 001, one of the most ancient Martian meteorites ever found on Earth. While scientists can never know for sure where a Martian meteorite originated, Teghaza 001 includes clues that link it to highlands in the southern hemisphere of […] Fuente: NASA.

item.description: Nature, Published online: 30 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03512-2 Fossils of dinosaurs, mammals and other glamorous species are over-represented in high-profile titles, suggests a study of thousands of palaeontology papers. Fuente: Nature.

item.title: Evolutionary changes in key enzyme may help bacteria make proteins faster
item.description: Evolutionary changes in a key protein synthesis enzyme, isoleucyl-tRNA synthetase (IleRS), may help bacteria fine-tune how quickly proteins are made, report researchers from Institute of Science Tokyo, Japan; the University of Zagreb Faculty of Science, Croatia; and ETH Zürich, Switzerland. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Using machine learning to build safer cities
item.description: In eThekwini, researchers have harnessed machine learning and satellite data to spot the city's most landslide-prone zones. A new study published in Scientific Reports has found that urban development activities, including road construction, property development and vegetation loss, are significantly increasing landslide susceptibility across parts of eThekwini. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Slice of Martian Meteorite Teghaza 001
item.description: Description This slice of Teghaza 001, one of the most ancient Martian meteorites ever found on Earth, was used to determine the age of the rock. Reflected light images like these serve as a scientist’s road map, helping them find minerals of interest to analyze by different instruments. Figure A is the same image with […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: How ancient insect-eating diets could inspire more sustainable food systems
item.description: New research from Durham University highlights how insects have been part of human diets for thousands of years despite seeming unusual to many people. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Rare 4.1-billion-year-old Martian meteorite reveals clues to planet's ancient past
item.description: Scientists at the University of New Mexico have played a key role in identifying a rare, 4.1-billion-year-old Martian meteorite that provides new evidence that the red planet may have once had a wetter, Earth-like environment. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Electrical guardrails for charge carriers: A new approach to harness graphene for solar cells
item.description: Graphene is a single layer of carbon atoms in which electrons can move with high mobility, making it promising for high-speed electronic components. Yet it is not very efficient at converting light into electricity. While light absorbed by graphene does excite electrons, leaving behind positively charged carriers called 'holes,' the absorbed light energy cannot be harnessed effectively unless electrons and holes are separated and directed to different contacts. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Faraway tectonic forces may have accelerated the Gulf of California rifting
item.description: When the Baja California peninsula broke from mainland Mexico nearly 12 million years ago, it gave rise to the Gulf of California. New research suggests that this process of continental rifting was greatly accelerated due to tectonic forces on the opposite side of the Pacific Ocean. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Simplified ancestral enzyme makes ATP without amino acid needed for its usual reaction
item.description: Proteins perform essential functions in living organisms, from catalyzing biochemical reactions to supporting cellular energy metabolism. Their functions depend on their amino acid composition and three-dimensional structures. However, early proteins may have evolved when fewer amino acid types were available than those used by most modern proteins. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New calculations reveal hidden pathways that let chemical reactions produce different products
item.description: Chemical reactions are often understood as molecules crossing a high-energy saddle point, known as a transition state, before following a downhill pathway toward a product. Conventional quantum chemical calculations typically trace this single pathway to determine how a reaction proceeds. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Asteroids venturing near white dwarfs don't break directly into dust, study reveals
item.description: When asteroids travel too close to white dwarfs, the dense remnants of stars that have exhausted their nuclear fuel, powerful gravitational forces can tear them apart. However, new research from Planetary Science Institute (PSI) suggests that these asteroids don't immediately break into dust. Instead, most of the mass initially remains in larger fragments, revealing a previously overlooked step in how debris forms around dying stars. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Sex after baby: How childhood trauma can get in the way
item.description: Why do some parents have more sexual difficulties than others after having a baby? Childhood trauma plays a significant role, amplifying the other factors at play. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Measuring multiple reactions on a single electrode with extraordinary sensitivity
item.description: A reaction on a single electrode can tell scientists a remarkable amount about the chemical nature and number of analytes involved. The challenge comes when they want to distinguish many reactions on the same electrode. After more than a decade of trying to overcome that limitation, Ravi Saraf and his Nebraska Engineering graduate students have demonstrated a way to quantify many reactions on the same electrode without sacrificing extraordinary sensitivity. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A protein that regulates mRNA decoding can itself be regulated with implications for understanding cancer
item.description: Decoding of messenger RNA (mRNA) occurs during translation, the vital cellular process that builds proteins. Errors in this process are known to lead to cancer growth. Scientists at St. Jude Children's Research Hospital identified how one factor involved in mRNA decoding can be altered, identifying potential cancer origins and new targets for KRAS-related treatment resistance. The results are published in Nature Cell Biology. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Researchers observe the arrival of El Niño in Monterey Bay
item.description: For more than 30 years, MBARI technology has recorded real-time data about Monterey Bay, from oceanographic conditions at the surface to biological surveys in the depths of Monterey Canyon. These data are integral to understanding our changing ocean and underpin the institute's efforts to monitor the impacts of the incoming El Niño, which has been predicted to be among the strongest since the beginning of modern oceanography. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Chinese scientists dissatisfied with jobs but optimistic about future, survey says
item.description: Chinese scientists are less satisfied with their jobs than researchers in any other major country, according to a survey that also found they are more optimistic about their careers than their counterparts in the United States and Britain. Only 51 per cent of the 157 respondents from China said they were satisfied with their jobs, according to the survey published this month in the British scientific journal Nature, down 24 per cent from 2018. The survey drew 3,882 respondents from 133... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Zhang Tong

item.title: Waves alter Antarctic polynyas by breaking up surrounding sea ice
item.description: Polynyas are one of Antarctica's great counterintuitive features: recurring areas of open water surrounded by vast expanses of sea ice. These unusual environments are hot spots for sea-ice production, ocean–atmosphere exchange and biological productivity. They are commonly maintained by powerful winds that push newly formed ice away from the coast, repeatedly exposing the ocean to the freezing Antarctic atmosphere. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Chemical recycling turns silicone waste into reusable building blocks with up to 99% yield
item.description: Silicones are widely used in industry, medicine and everyday products due to their exceptional thermal and chemical stability. However, it is precisely these properties that have made recycling silicones extremely problematic in the past. Researchers at the Institute of Chemistry at TU Berlin have now succeeded in breaking down the polymer chains of silicone molecules into their basic building blocks. The resulting molecule dimethyldichlorosilane can then be reused as a starting material for the production of new silicone compounds. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: A new study has pieced together the evolutionary history of terrestrial animals on the Qinghai–Tibet Plateau (QTP), offering a comprehensive picture of how the distinctive fauna of the "Third Pole" took shape over millions of years. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The human surfaceome: AI flags potential cell surface drug targets overlooked by major databases
item.description: More than 65% of approved medicines work by binding to proteins on the surface of human cells. Yet scientists developing new treatments face a fundamental problem: Major biological databases disagree about which proteins are actually found on cell surfaces. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Halloween Aboard the International Space Station
item.description: Although no ghouls, goblins, or trick-or-treaters come knocking at the International Space Station’s front hatch, crew members aboard the orbiting laboratory still like to get in the Halloween spirit. Whether individually or as an entire crew, they dress up in sometimes spooky, sometimes scary, but always creative costumes, often designed from materials available aboard the […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Sumer Loggins

item.title: The 'shape' of gene expression: Identifying genes that may share roles across species
item.description: Much of what we know about biology comes from animal models, particularly mice. Applying these insights to humans, however, is not always straightforward. For example, some of the genes important for the formation of germ cells, which eventually give rise to eggs or sperm, differ between mice and humans. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Nature finance needs a fundamental rethink, researchers argue
item.description: The authors call on governments, investors and conservation organizers to reimagine nature finance based on a central tenet: raising funds should be a means to an end, not an end in itself. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How the quantum vacuum perturbs atoms, could shrink black holes and may have helped form galaxies
item.description: The word "vacuum" may conjure the image of empty space. Maybe you think of a region far outside the solar system without planets, debris, gas clouds or light. According to quantum theory, however, a vacuum is never truly empty. Quantum mechanics extends the Heisenberg uncertainty principle—which states that we cannot measure the position and the velocity of an object exactly at the same time—to a vacuum. The result is that a vacuum can never be still. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Detailed images reveal ribosome assembly inside human cells for the first time
item.description: For decades, ribosomes have been under the lens of many scientists. Ribosomes are highly sophisticated and complex molecular machines that allow cells to synthesize proteins. However, putting ribosomes together requires intricate assembly processes. While many underlying mechanisms for building ribosomes have been discovered ex situ (outside their native cellular context), our understanding of how ribosomes are assembled in situ has so far remained limited. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Eyewitnesses remember feedback better after making an identification, study finds
item.description: An eyewitness can tell the truth, believe every word they say and still send an innocent person to prison. A new study by Stephen Charman from FIU's Department of Psychology takes on a question that has challenged the justice system for decades: Can we rely on eyewitnesses to help identify the person responsible for a crime? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Terahertz light distinguishes two groups of particles trapped inside superconducting vortices
item.description: Scientists at Rutgers and in Estonia have used invisible light to look into tiny magnetic whirlpools, called vortices, inside a superconductor, revealing details that could help researchers develop better materials for carrying electricity. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: What animal bones in Malawi teach us about the social lives of people long ago
item.description: In the ancient past, when human communities were small and the only way to travel was by walking, what were the chances of meeting a stranger? And what would happen next? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: European rivers retain far more plastic than they carry to the sea, study finds
item.description: Plastic that enters the environment does not necessarily make its way to the sea via rivers. In fact, only a tiny fraction eventually reaches river mouths. Most plastic remains on land or within river systems. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Wild orchids face growing challenges as conservation falls short
item.description: At first glance, it is easy to see why Corybas puniceus has captured the attention of collectors around the world. Small enough to fit in the palm of your hand, its unusual shape and bursts of color make it unlike almost anything else in the orchid world. The species, found only in Southeast Asia, is classified as critically endangered. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How eggs protect chromosome connections during prolonged dormancy
item.description: Eggs follow a very different developmental path from sperm. Once a male hits puberty, sperm cells are produced continuously throughout his life. Eggs, however, are all produced during the fetal stage. Once formed, eggs enter a long dormant state called the dictyate stage, in which the process of cell division (meiosis) is paused partway through. This dormant period ends only when the egg is ovulated. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Sealing gaps and securing food can fight rodent infestations while protecting predators
item.description: Mice and rats can spread dangerous viruses and bacteria, trigger asthma attacks and damage property with their constant gnawing. So when rodents get indoors, most people take action to help keep their home safe. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Machine learning helps track semiconductor defects under more realistic temperature conditions
item.description: All materials contain inherent defects. These are not always harmful, since they can be used to engineer and introduce certain properties into a material. However, it is crucial to understand how they function and how they affect the material's properties. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: As farm fuel costs rise, clear solar might offer a solution
item.description: Researchers from Charles Sturt University are investigating how transparent solar panels can help power the future of Australian agriculture. Fuente: ABC News Australia.
item.dc:creator: Melinda Hayter and Emily Doak

item.title: What killed 500-plus penguins? How scientists solved the mystery
item.description: The penguins that perished lived on the Danger Islands in Antarctica. The prime suspect was avian flu. Researchers were surprised by what they found. Fuente: NPR - World.
item.dc:creator: Gabrielle Emanuel

item.title: HomeownerPal ha comentado: The Cliffs of Insanity, but with a much better view. Inconceivable that this is real!
item.description: The rugged summits of the Cordillera del Paine mountain range pierce the sky in Torres del Paine National Park, Chile. Fuente: National Geographic.

item.title: Astronauts Anil Menon and Joshua Kutryk completed a spacewalk at 3:08 p.m. EDT today after installing a roll-out solar array for power generation. They will conduct a f... Ver más
item.description: Astronauts Anil Menon and Joshua Kutryk completed a spacewalk at 3:08 p.m. EDT today after installing a roll-out solar array for power generation. They will conduct a f... Ver más International Space Station Hace 24 minutos 24 min · Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Newly discovered amoeba reproduces at 145 F, breaking heat record for eukaryotic life
item.description: Organisms are products of the environments they live and evolve in. While the physical world is governed by universal laws like thermodynamics and gravity, there are few laws of biology. An open question for biologists like me is how environmental conditions shape what organisms look like and dictate how they live, breathe and move. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Planetary collisions may help young worlds hold on to their atmospheres
item.description: A new study lets some of the air out of a long-held theory that growing, rocky planets will lose their atmosphere if they smash into a large object in space. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 3,700-year-old man buried with stone in his mouth beneath a hearth may have been part of magical ritual
item.description: Approximately 3,700 years ago, a man in southeastern Spain underwent a burial unlike any other. Researchers suggest that this ritual may have been intended to symbolically overcome a threat rather than inflict punishment. The discovery of his body underneath a hearth, with a stone in his mouth, implies an effort to silence him. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: Fresh as the microplastic-laden Sierra snow: Storms can deliver pollution to even remote locations
item.description: For the first time, UC Riverside scientists have measured how much microplastic pollution falls on the Sierra Nevada during snowstorms and were surprised to find significant amounts even in the most remote locations. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Light reshapes gelatin scaffolds to steer cell growth in three dimensions
item.description: Soft, flexible hydrogels have enabled significant advancements in engineering biological tissue by mimicking the natural scaffolding that provides structure and support to cells. Existing engineered hydrogels, however, fall short in a significant way. Unlike in nature, they do not have the dynamic ability to change their structure or support depending on what the biological tissue needs. The answer may rest in shining a light on the problem—literally, according to a team led by researchers at Yokohama National University. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Political information increasingly comes from pop culture
item.description: Research on political polarization points to how people's preferred news outlets and social media use create information silos, environments in which people primarily encounter views consistent with their own, further cementing those views. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The rugged summits of the Cordillera del Paine mountain range pierce the sky in Torres del Paine National Park, Chile.
item.description: The rugged summits of the Cordillera del Paine mountain range pierce the sky in Torres del Paine National Park, Chile. The Cliffs of Insanity, but with a much better view. Inconceivable that this is real! HomeownerPal Fuente: National Geographic.

item.title: Experimental study on moths supports the molecular cookie cutter idea proposed for butterflies
item.description: Have you ever thought about reinventing yourself? According to a new study on moths conducted by Andrei Sourakov, collection coordinator of Lepidoptera at the Florida Museum of Natural History and affiliate associate professor of entomology at the University of Florida, it's not as hard as you might think. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Is it a boy or a girl? For alligators, it may come down to one degree
item.description: The future of the alligator species could come down to a one- or two-degree temperature difference, according to new research from the University of Georgia. The findings are published in the Journal of Experimental Biology. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A blue laser for underwater communication and sensing
item.description: Researchers at EPFL have developed a chip-scale blue laser that combines stable light emission with rapid frequency control, opening possibilities for underwater communication, environmental sensing and quantum technologies. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Built to take the blast: Students test prototype landing pad to make moon landings safer
item.description: As NASA works toward a sustained human presence on the moon, researchers at The University of Alabama in Huntsville (UAH), a part of The University of Alabama System, are helping solve one of the most pressing challenges facing future lunar missions: how to land spacecraft safely without damaging the landing vehicle or nearby infrastructure. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Key Atlantic currents could collapse this century, but the risk is missing from almost all national climate plans
item.description: Icelandic government officials recently met to discuss a dramatic scenario: what if the current that circulates Atlantic waters weakened significantly, or collapsed altogether? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Famed oceanographer calls for ending krill catch near Antarctica as governments debate fishing quota
item.description: Renowned oceanographer Sylvia Earle is calling for an end to krill fishing near Antarctica as officials from the U.S., China, Russia and 24 other governments negotiate a possible deal to dramatically expand fishing for the crustacean that's a vital food source for whales in the international waters surrounding the ice-covered continent. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Nighttime songs could reveal when endangered pygmy blue whales feed off Western Australia
item.description: Listening to the songs of endangered pygmy blue whales could help researchers identify when the animals are feeding off Western Australia's coast, improving scientists' ability to monitor their behavior and inform conservation efforts. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA-funded Study Details One of Oldest Mars Meteorites Ever Found
item.description: When a rose-colored meteorite was found in the Sahara Desert in 2022, no one knew how old it was or where it came from. Not until NASA-funded scientists age-dated its minerals did they realize the nearly 2-pound (800-gram) rock was a piece of Mars that formed more than 4.1 billion years ago, making it one […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Amanda Barnett

item.title: Researchers create first whole-body single-cell atlas of an adult vertebrate
item.description: Viewed from above, Danionella cerebrum offers a rare sight in a vertebrate: its brain, visible through the top of its head. Since the species was adopted for neuroscience research in 2018 and formally described in 2021, the tiny, transparent fish has drawn rapidly growing interest for its unique biology. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Birds and humans share fundamental song and speech patterns, study finds
item.description: McGill University researchers have identified "universal" vocal patterns across hundreds of bird species and found that many of the same patterns also appear in human song and speech from cultures around the world. The patterns include small pitch intervals, regular and predictable rhythms, and phrase-final elongation, in which the last utterance in a phrase tends to be longer than the others. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Long-distance flights can throw seabirds' internal clocks out of sync, causing navigation errors
item.description: A study led by Oxford University has found that seabirds flying long distances across the Atlantic can experience a mismatch between their internal body clocks and local time (the same process that leads to jet lag in humans), causing them to make predictable errors when navigating by the sun. The results have been published in the journal Science. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA Names Troy Asher Armstrong Flight Research Center Director
item.description: NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman has named Troy Asher director of the agency’s Armstrong Flight Research Center in Edwards, California. Asher, a veteran test pilot and aerospace engineer with decades of experience in flight research and operations, has served as the center’s acting director since March. “Troy has spent his career pushing the boundaries of flight, […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Lauren E. Low

item.title: Analysis of Córdoba's urban trees identifies which species best tolerate heat
item.description: The orange tree emerges as one of the most heat-vulnerable trees, according to a University of Córdoba (UCO) study that analyzed 17 tree species found in Córdoba's urban environment. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Global maps reveal farming, dams and agricultural runoff as leading threats to freshwater species
item.description: Farming, dams and agricultural runoff are the biggest threats to freshwater biodiversity globally, with Europe and Northwest Africa the hardest-hit regions, McGill researchers have found. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: AI helps uncover overlooked 2D materials and create 11 new ones
item.description: With the help of artificial intelligence, researchers at Linköping University in Sweden have found previously overlooked occurrences of the 2D materials MXenes in older databases. The findings have inspired the researchers to create new materials using more sustainable synthesis methods. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: One molecule, many atoms: Platinum bonds respond to surface features up to 10 nanometers away
item.description: Many chemical processes that sustain modern society depend on molecules binding to metal surfaces. The production of synthetic fertilizer, for example, relies on heterogeneous catalysis, in which gases react on the surface of a solid catalyst. Yet, until now, an important question has remained unresolved: How much of the metal surface actually participates in determining the strength of a chemical bond on the surface? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NIH–NASA QuSAFE Challenge
item.description: The Quantum-Enabled Predictive Preclinical NAMs for Toxicity and Safety (QuSAFE) Challenge, a collaboration between the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and NASA, advances quantum-enabled sensing for in vitro NAMs, such as organoids and microphysiological systems (MPS), to improve drug safety while reducing animal use. In vitro NAMs, such as organoids and microphysiological systems (MPS), can […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Bailey Light

item.title: Unusual whale sightings around Australia may signal changing ocean conditions
item.description: Whales never cease to amaze me. After nearly two decades of studying these majestic mammals, I've learned every whale season is slightly different. Each migration along Australia's east coast varies in its timing and the number of whale sightings. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Newly characterized Streptomyces strain yields previously unknown natural products
item.description: In a collaboration, researchers from the Leibniz Institute DSMZ-German Collection of Microorganisms and Cell Cultures and the Helmholtz Center for Infection Research (HZI) have discovered two previously unknown natural products. Lavasamycin A and B are produced by the bacterium Streptomyces barkulensis subsp. lavasanensis, which was isolated from a soil sample collected in Lavasan, Iran, and characterized as a new subspecies at the DSMZ. The findings have been published in the Journal of Natural Products. Fuente: Phys.org.
